title: Twenty First Word First Station Conclusion Worldly Deception Death And The Grave

questions.question: What main warning is given in this conclusion about loving worldly life too much?
questions.answer: Being fooled by this life can make a person forget the hereafter and live in heedlessness.

questions.question: Which part of a person is being addressed in this passage?
questions.answer: The lower self, or nafs, is being addressed.

questions.question: How is the nafs described at the beginning of the passage?
questions.answer: It is described as careless, attached to this life, and forgetful of the next life.

questions.question: What animal is used in the comparison?
questions.answer: An ostrich.

questions.question: Why does the ostrich put its head in the sand in the comparison?
questions.answer: It is trying to avoid facing the hunter.

questions.question: Why does that action not actually save the ostrich?
questions.answer: Its body is still exposed, so the danger has not gone away.

questions.question: What is the point of saying the ostrich cannot see the hunter?
questions.answer: It shows that closing your eyes to danger does not remove the danger.

questions.question: According to the passage, what has the heedless nafs forgotten?
questions.answer: It has forgotten the hereafter.

questions.question: What does the nafs seek instead of the hereafter?
questions.answer: It chases only this world.

questions.question: What Qur’anic message is placed at the start of the conclusion about worldly things?
questions.answer: It teaches that the attractions of this world are deceptive and cannot be trusted as lasting success.

questions.question: What does the passage say is wrong with the nafs’s view of life?
questions.answer: It sees worldly life as pleasing and enough by itself.

questions.question: What important reality has the nafs neglected?
questions.answer: It has neglected the hereafter.

questions.question: What does the nafs focus on instead?
questions.answer: It focuses only on this worldly life.

questions.question: What creature is used to make this lesson easier to understand?
questions.answer: An ostrich is used.

questions.question: What danger appears in the example with the ostrich?
questions.answer: A hunter appears.

questions.question: How does the ostrich respond to the hunter?
questions.answer: It hides its head instead of escaping properly.

questions.question: In the comparison, what remains uncovered even after the ostrich hides its head?
questions.answer: Its large body remains uncovered.

questions.question: What does the hunter still do despite the ostrich’s action?
questions.answer: The hunter still sees it.

questions.question: What does the ostrich fail to do because its eyes are buried?
questions.answer: It fails to see the danger clearly.

questions.question: In this passage, what is the biggest spiritual problem of the nafs?
questions.answer: Its biggest problem is heedlessness.

questions.question: How does heedlessness affect the nafs’s priorities?
questions.answer: It makes worldly life seem sweetest and pushes the hereafter out of mind.

questions.question: What is the nafs mainly chasing in the passage?
questions.answer: It is chasing worldly life alone.

questions.question: What comparison is used to expose the nafs’s mistake?
questions.answer: The nafs is compared to an ostrich.

questions.question: What truth is the heedless nafs refusing to face?
questions.answer: It is refusing to face the reality of the hereafter and the emptiness of living only for this world.

questions.question: Why does the passage say, in meaning, “think about this example”?
questions.answer: It wants the listener to reflect deeply, not just hear the words and move on.

questions.question: What does the verse at the beginning teach about the life of this world?
questions.answer: It teaches that worldly possessions and pleasures can deceive people.

questions.question: Who is being warned directly in the passage?
questions.answer: The speaker’s own nafs is being warned directly.

questions.question: What three traits of the nafs are mentioned before the comparison?
questions.answer: It is heedless, attracted to worldly sweetness, and forgetful of the hereafter.

questions.question: What does the nafs want most, according to the passage?
questions.answer: It wants this world only.

questions.question: What is the purpose of comparing the nafs to an ostrich?
questions.answer: It is to show how foolish it is to avoid reality instead of dealing with it.

questions.question: What danger stands for a threat in the ostrich example?
questions.answer: The hunter stands for the threat.

questions.question: What does the ostrich do because it cannot escape in a better way?
questions.answer: It pushes its head into the sand.

questions.question: What lesson does this teach about denial?
questions.answer: Denial may hide the truth from a person’s attention, but it does not change the truth.

questions.question: What false idea about worldly life is being challenged in this passage?
questions.answer: The false idea that this world is satisfying on its own and worth living for by itself.

questions.question: What happens to the nafs when it is drowned in heedlessness?
questions.answer: It becomes attached to worldly pleasures and forgets the next life.

questions.question: Which future reality is ignored by such a nafs?
questions.answer: The hereafter is ignored.

questions.question: What simple image is used to uncover this mistake?
questions.answer: The image of an ostrich and a hunter is used.

questions.question: What does the ostrich hope to gain by putting its head in the sand?
questions.answer: It hopes to feel safe by blocking out the threat.

questions.question: Why is that hope empty?
questions.answer: The danger remains present whether or not the ostrich looks at it.

questions.question: What part of the ostrich shows that hiding is incomplete?
questions.answer: Its large body is still left outside.

questions.question: In a spiritual sense, what is like putting one’s head in the sand?
questions.answer: Ignoring the hereafter and living only for worldly desires is like that.

questions.question: What is the passage asking the nafs to do instead of hiding?
questions.answer: It is asking the nafs to reflect honestly on its condition.

questions.question: What main moral lesson ties the whole passage together?
questions.answer: A person should not let love of this world blind him to eternal truth.

questions.question: What does the opening verse say about the things of this world in general?
questions.answer: They are temporary attractions that can mislead people.

questions.question: What has made this nafs spiritually unhealthy?
questions.answer: Its love of worldly life and neglect of the hereafter have made it unhealthy.

questions.question: What does the nafs wrongly treat as its main goal?
questions.answer: It treats this world as its main goal.

questions.question: What example from nature is used to correct this attitude?
questions.answer: The passage uses an ostrich facing a hunter.

questions.question: What makes the ostrich’s behavior unreasonable?
questions.answer: It responds to danger with pretend hiding instead of real safety.

questions.question: What does burying its head fail to change?
questions.answer: It fails to change the fact that the hunter still sees and can catch it.

questions.question: What does the ostrich lose by hiding its eyes?
questions.answer: It loses awareness of the threat while still remaining in danger.

questions.question: What two realities are placed in contrast in this passage?
questions.answer: The passing world is contrasted with the hereafter.

questions.question: Which one has the heedless nafs forgotten?
questions.answer: It has forgotten the hereafter.

questions.question: What does the instruction to consider the comparison encourage?
questions.answer: It encourages serious thinking and honest self-judgment.
